title: רב כהנא

paragraphs: (a) Rav's student-colleague, like Rav Assi—Rashi, Shabbat (146b); Rosh, chapter HaMokher Et HaBayit, and Tosafot, Ḥullin (19a), write likewise. They were senior to Rav Huna and Shemuel. In chapter Eḥad Dinei Mamonot (36b), he needed Rav's received teaching, but not his reasoning. In Shabbat (152a), he recited the orders before Rav. Bava Metzia (64a): Rav Kahana said, 'I was sitting at the end of Rav's lecture.' At the beginning of Bammeh Ishah, he asked Rav. Jerusalem Talmud, chapter Mitzvat Ḥalitzah: Rav Kahana's maternal uncle, etc.; Rav heard and said, etc. In HaRo'eh (62a), Ḥagigah (5b), he lay beneath Rav's bed and heard him converse and have intercourse. He said, 'Abba's mouth seems like one who has not tasted cooked food.' Rav said, 'Leave; this is not proper conduct.' He answered, 'It is Torah, and I need to learn.'

(b) He went up to the Land of Israel twice. Once he encountered R. Shimon son of Rabbi, as in Zevaḥim, chapter Kodshei Kodashim (59); the second time was in R. Yoḥanan's days, when R. Yoḥanan was old. Tosafot, Menaḥot 23b [printed locator: כ״נ, end of side b], says Rav Kahana went up several times. Tosafot, Sukkah (44a), says that when he went up, R. Yoḥanan headed the academy; presumably R. Yoḥanan did not head it throughout the lifetime of his teacher Ḥizkiyah son of R. Ḥiyya. Although HaKometz Rabbah has Rav Kahana encountering R. Ḥiyya's sons when he went up, perhaps he ascended twice, once in Ḥizkiyah's days and once in R. Yoḥanan's. Tosafot there writes likewise. In HaMegaresh (84b), they write that presumably Ḥizkiyah, R. Yoḥanan's teacher, had already died when Rav Kahana went up. Had Ḥizkiyah lived, Rav Kahana would not have left him to sit before R. Yoḥanan, nor would R. Yoḥanan have headed an academy while Ḥizkiyah lived. See Tosafot, Bava Kamma (117b). Yet Kodshei Kodashim says Rav Kahana encountered R. Shimon son of Rabbi, who was senior even to R. Ḥiyya, Ḥizkiyah's father. How could Rav Kahana leave him to learn before R. Yoḥanan? Therefore it appears that he went up twice. End of quotation. According to the foregoing—that he went up in the days of R. Shimon son of Rabbi, Ḥizkiyah, and R. Yoḥanan—he went up three times. This also follows from Tosafot in Menaḥot, which says 'several times.' At any rate, his ascent to R. Yoḥanan was the third. This is difficult to reconcile with the Jerusalem Talmud I shall cite shortly, according to which Rav Kahana was a child and youth when he went up to R. Yoḥanan. Bava Kamma (117): Rav Kahana killed an informer who showed an idolater how to take his fellow's straw. Rav told him to go up to the Land of Israel and undertake not to challenge R. Yoḥanan for seven years. When he arrived, Resh Lakish told R. Yoḥanan, 'A lion has come up from Babylonia'; R. Yoḥanan should review his academy teaching. The next day they seated Rav Kahana in the first row. R. Yoḥanan stated a teaching, and he did not object; another teaching, and he did not object, until they placed him behind seven rows. R. Yoḥanan told Resh Lakish, 'The lion you mentioned has become a fox.' Rav Kahana said, 'May these seven rows substitute for the seven years I undertook not to challenge R. Yoḥanan.' He rose and said, 'Let the master return to the beginning.' He stated a teaching and Rav Kahana objected, another teaching and he objected, until they placed him in the first row. R. Yoḥanan sat on seven cushions; he removed them all until he sat on the ground. He was an old man with drooping eyebrows and said, 'Lift my eyes so I can see him.' Seeing Rav Kahana's parted lips, he thought he was laughing at him, felt hurt, and Rav Kahana died. R. Yoḥanan said, 'See how the Babylonian behaves!' They told him, 'That is his usual appearance.' He went to the cave, which a snake encircled. He said, 'Snake, open your mouth, and let a teacher enter to his student.' It did not open. He said, 'Let a colleague enter to his colleague.' It did not open. He said, 'Let a student enter to his teacher.' It opened. He prayed and revived him, saying, 'Had I known that this was the master's appearance, I would not have felt hurt. Now let the master come with us.' He answered, 'If you can pray that I will not die again, I shall go; otherwise, no.' He raised him, asked all his uncertainties, and Rav Kahana resolved them. This is what R. Yoḥanan meant: ‘I thought it was yours. It is theirs’ [Rashi in Bava Kamma understands this of Torah learning. See also the interpretation cited below.]. See Rashi in HaMegaresh there. Rashi in Bava Kamma there writes: Pesaḥim (49) proves that Rav Kahana returned home, for he said, 'Had I not married a priest's daughter, I would not have been exiled.' They said, 'But you were exiled to a place of Torah!' He answered, 'I was not exiled as people are: I did not go for Torah, but for fear of the government.' Thus he lived afterward. Moreover, Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, HaYah Kore, mishnah 8, says a man encountered him and asked, 'What is happening in heaven?'—mocking his having died and revived. He answered, 'That man's sentence is sealed,' and the man died. Another encountered him, spoke likewise, and died. He came before R. Yoḥanan and said, 'A person whose mother ... and whose father's wife honors him,' etc. End of Rashi's quotation. It is surprising: how does this prove he lived afterward? I heard from the distinguished Rabbi Alexander, in the name of the eminent Rabbi Heshel: how did Rav Kahana know he was exiled for marrying a priest's daughter? Rather, after dying he heard in heaven that this was why he died. These are the words of a wise man's mouth. Yet perhaps he said this immediately upon arriving in the Land of Israel, before R. Yoḥanan punished him; one can reconcile this. In my opinion, an undesignated 'they said to him' means his students said it. Had he said, 'Had I not married a priest's daughter, I would not have been exiled,' immediately upon arrival, before dying, how could his students say, 'But you were exiled to a place of Torah'? R. Yoḥanan punished him the very next day; whence did he then have students? Necessarily he returned to Babylonia, as the Jerusalem Talmud there explicitly relates: they told R. Yoḥanan that Kahana had gone down to Babylonia. He asked why he had not requested permission. They answered: he asked you where one should go if his mother despises him (the Land of Israel is compared to a mother), while his father's wife (Babylonia) honors him. R. Yoḥanan answered: where he is honored—meaning Babylonia. This constituted taking leave. End of quotation. Upon returning to Babylonia he had students there, and they said, 'But to a place of Torah,' etc. I see another proof that he returned home, from that Jerusalem Talmud: 'Kahana was olam saggin when he came up here. A scoundrel saw him and asked, "What news in heaven?" He answered, "The sentence,"' etc.; another likewise encountered him, as above. Yuḥasin, order of amoraim, letter alef, under Rav Assi, writes that Rav Kahana was a child and youth when he went up to R. Yoḥanan, as in the Jerusalem Talmud. It does not identify the location. In my opinion it means the foregoing: 'Kahana was olam saggin when he went up; a worthless fellow saw him and asked, "What news in the world?" He answered, "That man's sentence,"' etc. After writing this I found it explicit in Asheri, Asarah Yuḥasin: the Jerusalem Talmud's olam saggin means a child and youth. This pleased me. The commentary on the Jerusalem Talmud and Penei Moshe explain olam saggin as meaning: since he is diligent and cleaves to God, he should tell me what news there is in heaven—diligent in Torah and commandments. End of quotation. He erred: on that interpretation it should say, 'A worthless fellow saw him and said: Olam saggin, what news?'—you who are wise and diligent in Torah, tell me what news you heard in heaven. His explanation of 'What news in heaven?' as 'What news have you now heard in heaven?' is also erroneous. Could he find no sage of the Land of Israel to ask for this prophecy? Rather, as Rashi explains, he asked what he heard in heaven while dead. Thus, when R. Yoḥanan punished him he was a child and youth. Jerusalem Talmud, Rosh HaShanah 2, halakhah 6, and Sanhedrin 1, halakhah 2, relates: R. Ḥiyya bar Abba, R. Yoḥanan's student, stood praying. Rav Kahana entered and prayed behind him. When R. Ḥiyya finished he sat, so as not to pass before him. Rav Kahana prolonged his prayer. When he finished, R. Ḥiyya asked, 'What is your practice where you live—do you distress great men?' He answered, 'My teacher, I am of Eli's house, of which it is written, "The iniquity of Eli's house shall not be expiated by sacrifice or offering." It is not expiated by sacrifice or offering, but is expiated through prayer.' He prayed for him, and he merited growing old until his nails became red like a דקקה [comparison unresolved] (meaning he became so old that his nails reddened from age). This proves he lived afterward into old age and did not die as a child. The Jerusalem Talmud also explicitly says he took leave of R. Yoḥanan to return to Babylonia. This is an unanswerable proof; it is surprising that Rashi, light of the exile, did not cite it. He left room [for others]. Yet I saw in Gelilot Eretz Yisrael that he saw the graves of R. Yoḥanan and Rav Kahana in Tiberias; this requires examination.

(c) He was very beautiful: Rav Kahana's beauty resembled Rav's, Rav's resembled R. Abbahu's (Bava Metzia 84a lacks 'Rav's, and Rav's resembled'), R. Abbahu's [abbreviated ר״א] resembled Jacob's, and Jacob's resembled Adam's, Bava Batra (58a).

(d) It is doubtful whether he was a priest. In Ḥullin (132a), Rav Kahana ate on his wife's account. Tosafot writes that the Rav Kahana who was exiled was not a priest, while the second was. Pesaḥim (49a): 'Had I not married a priest's daughter, I would not have been exiled'; see Tosafot on side b. Certainly the exile was the first Rav Kahana, for the second, in Rav Ashi's time, was a priest: Kiddushin, chapter 1 (8a), says he took a cloth for redemption of a firstborn. Tosafot there writes: he was a priest, or took the cloth on his wife's account. Tosafot Rid says there were two, one in Rav and R. Yoḥanan's time and one in Rav Ashi's; the first was not a priest. End of quotation. Elsewhere he seems to be a priest: Arvei Pesaḥim (113) and chapter Yesh Noḥalin (110) have Rav telling him, 'Skin a carcass in the marketplace and do not say, "I am Kahana."' Yet one can answer that he was renowned: do not say, 'I am Kahana; I am a great man,' etc. Ritva in Ein Yaakov writes likewise: was he not a non-priest, since he ate on his wife's account? Some explain there were two Rav Kahanas, but this is unnecessary: kahana denotes distinction; the correct explanation is that Rav spoke thus because his name was Kahana. Tosafot there likewise says he was not a priest. At the end of HaMotze Tefillin (Eruvin 105a [printed locator: ר״ה a]), Rav Huna says, 'Rav Kahana assists priests,' saying impure priests are preferable to pure Israelites. There are arguments both ways. Midrash Shemuel, at 'Therefore I swore to Eli's house,' relates Rav Kahana's prolonged prayer and R. Ḥiyya bar Abba's anger, etc. One cannot say R. Ḥiyya prayed for the second Rav Kahana, Rav Ashi's teacher: R. Ḥiyya was R. Yoḥanan's student, who lived in Rav's time; Rav taught Rav Yehudah, who died old when Rava was born, and Rav Ashi was born when Rava died. How could R. Ḥiyya pray for the second Kahana, Rav Ashi's teacher? Rav Kahana said he belonged to Eli's house, as in the Jerusalem Talmud above. It seems explicit that he was a priest. I say, however, that if this is the reason, one can answer as Rashi does in Rosh HaShanah (18): Rava and Abaye both descended from Eli. Abaye, who engaged in Torah and kindness, lived sixty years; Rava, who engaged only in Torah, forty. Rashi explains that chapter HaZeroa shows Rava was not a priest; perhaps his mother descended from Eli. End of quotation. Thus descent from Eli does not prove Rav Kahana was a priest: it could be maternal. See below for the statement in Gilgulei Neshamot that he was not a priest. Since he lived so long, as above, one might say the Kahana of Rav's and Rav Ashi's days was one person. But this is not so: Kahana spoke to Rav Ashi in Rava's name. How could Rav's student-colleague speak in Rava's name? There must have been two. Nevertheless his priesthood remains undecided: the cloth too could have been received on his wife's account, as Tosafot says. This requires examination.

(e) 'Rav Kahana said,' etc., 'R. Yoḥanan said,' etc., Bava Kamma (58a). Why is Rav Kahana placed before R. Yoḥanan, who was older? See the rules; perhaps because he was sharper. Tosafot, Ḥagigah (10, beginning of side a), says Rav Kahana fasted to forget the Babylonian Talmud. It seems a scribal error, for we find this only concerning R. Zeira; see there. Rav told him, 'Judge our host.' He was presumptuous; Rav Kahana said, 'If you do not obey, I shall remove Rav from your ear'—Rashi explains: I shall excommunicate you—Sanhedrin (8a). She'erit Yosef, Netiv HaPoresh, rule 6, writes: objections are raised from Rav Kahana despite his being an amora, as from Rav and Shemuel, because he was a great man; Abaye is among the later amoraim, so objections are not raised from him. Tosafot, Mo'ed Katan (2, end of side b), writes likewise: although Rav Kahana is an amora, objections are raised from him against Rabbah and Rav Yosef because he was great, as the R. Yoḥanan incident shows his extreme sharpness. End of quotation. Yuḥasin writes in Rav Sherira Gaon's name: Rav is a tanna and may disagree. There were also sages who were only amoraim, such as Shemuel, Rav Shila, Rabbah bar bar Ḥana, Rav Kahana, and Rav Assi; in their days, toward their end, Rav Adda bar Ahavah and Rabbah bar Abbahu were elders; see there. Kiddushin, end of chapter 1 (40a): Rav Kahana sold baskets. A matron solicited him. He said, 'I shall go adorn myself,' went up and fell from the roof to the ground. Elijah came and caught him, saying, 'You have troubled me four hundred parasangs.' He answered, 'What caused this? Poverty.' He gave him a vessel of dinars. Gilgulei Neshamot writes: the matron was Kozbi, and Rav Kahana a spark of Pinḥas son of Aaron the priest; now he was not a priest, for he said, 'Had I not married a priest's daughter,' etc. She wished to make him stumble in return for his killing her. Elijah came and caught him because of the relationship, as above, since Elijah is Pinḥas. End of quotation. In the Jerusalem Talmud, when he died he left R. Yoshiyah as heir, and R. Elazar wrote the will's witnesses [כתב עדי צוואה, construction provisional].
